q.s: A 45-year-old man has loss of taste over the anterior two-thirds of the tongue on the right after a middle ear operation. General sensation (touch, pain) on the same area is intact. Which nerve carries the lost taste fibers?
e: Wrong. V3 carries general sensation from the anterior 2/3, which is intact.
Correct. Taste from the anterior 2/3 of the tongue travels via the facial nerve (chorda tympani), which crosses the middle ear.
Wrong. CN IX carries taste and sensation from the posterior 1/3.
Wrong. CN X carries taste from the extreme posterior tongue and epiglottis.

q.s: The posterior one-third of the tongue develops from which pharyngeal arches?
e: Wrong. The 6th arch forms laryngeal structures.
Correct. The 3rd and 4th arches form the posterior 1/3, so sensation and taste are mainly via CN IX (extreme posterior via CN X).
Wrong. Contributes only to the anterior tongue.

q.s: A patient protrudes his tongue and it deviates to the left. Which muscle is weak?
e: Wrong. Retracts and elevates the sides.
Wrong. A weak right genioglossus causes deviation to the right.
Wrong. Elevates the posterior tongue (CN X).
Correct. Each genioglossus pushes the tongue forward and toward the opposite side; a weak left genioglossus (left CN XII lesion) lets the right side push the tongue to the left.

q.s: Which tongue muscle is innervated by the vagus nerve rather than the hypoglossal nerve?
e: Correct. Palatoglossus (elevates posterior tongue during swallowing) is supplied by CN X.

q.s: Taste information from the tongue converges on which brainstem nucleus?
o: Dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus
e: Wrong. Motor nucleus for pharynx and larynx.
Correct. Taste via CN VII, IX and X ends in the NTS.
Wrong. Pain and temperature from the face.

q.s: Pain sensation from the tongue is carried by which nerves?
e: Correct. Pain is carried by V3 (anterior 2/3), IX (posterior 1/3) and X (extreme posterior).

q.s: The foregut extends from the esophagus to which landmark?
o: The duodenum at the level of the ampulla of Vater
e: Correct. The foregut ends where the pancreatic and common bile ducts enter the duodenum.
Wrong. Midgut/hindgut boundary is at the distal transverse colon.
Wrong. The foregut includes the proximal duodenum.
Wrong. The midgut begins in the lower duodenum.

q.s: The midgut extends from the lower duodenum to which part of the colon?
o: The proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon
e: Correct. The midgut ends at the proximal 2/3 of the transverse colon; the hindgut begins at the distal 1/3.
Wrong. The midgut continues beyond the cecum.

q.s: The hindgut forms the distal transverse colon down to which landmark?
o: The anal canal above the pectinate line
e: Correct. Below the pectinate line is ectodermal.
Wrong. The hindgut continues to the anal canal.

q.s: During weeks 4–6, the stomach rotates 90° clockwise. Which consequence follows?
o: The liver rotates to the left
The right vagus nerve lies anterior to the stomach
The spleen moves to the right
The left vagus nerve becomes anterior and the right vagus posterior
e: Wrong. The right vagus becomes posterior.
Correct. Rotation moves the left vagus anteriorly and the right vagus posteriorly.

q.s: In the 6th week of development, which normal event occurs in the midgut?
o: Physiologic herniation through the umbilical ring
e: Correct. The midgut herniates in week 6 and returns in week 10.

q.s: As the midgut returns to the abdomen, it rotates around which axis and by how much?
e: Correct. The midgut rotates 270° counterclockwise around the SMA.

q.s: During physiologic herniation, the midgut is connected to the yolk sac by which structure?
e: Correct. Its persistence causes Meckel diverticulum.

q.s: An infant has a malrotation. Which artery is the normal axis of midgut rotation?
e: Wrong. A branch, not the axis.
Correct. The midgut rotates around the SMA.

q.s: The stomach, liver, gallbladder and proximal duodenum receive arterial supply mainly from which vessel?
e: Correct. Foregut structures are supplied by the celiac trunk.

q.s: The sigmoid colon is part of which embryologic division and receives which artery?
e: Correct. The hindgut (distal 1/3 transverse colon to upper anal canal) is supplied by the IMA.

q.s: A man has pain from an inflamed appendix felt initially around the umbilicus. This reflects the appendix's origin from which embryologic division?
e: Correct. Midgut visceral pain is referred to the periumbilical region.

q.s: A newborn's upper anal canal mucosa is endodermal, while the lower anal canal is ectodermal. Which landmark marks this transition?
e: Correct. Above it is hindgut endoderm; below it is ectoderm.

q.s: Which structure is derived from the midgut?
e: Correct. The jejunum and ileum are midgut.

q.s: Midgut return to the abdominal cavity occurs mainly during which week?
e: Correct. The midgut returns with the remaining 180° of rotation in week 10.

rounds.t: Ventral wall defects, TE fistula, pyloric stenosis, and atresia

q.s: Prenatal ultrasound shows free-floating loops of bowel to the right of a normally inserted umbilical cord, not covered by a membrane. Which statement is correct?
o: This is an umbilical hernia covered by skin
This is omphalocele, strongly associated with trisomy 18
This is gastroschisis, usually not associated with chromosomal abnormalities and with a good prognosis
e: Wrong. Omphalocele is midline and membrane-covered.
Correct. Gastroschisis is a right paraumbilical defect not covered by peritoneum or amnion.

q.s: A newborn has a midline abdominal wall defect at the umbilicus containing bowel and liver within a shiny gray sac. Which condition should be evaluated for?
e: Correct. Omphalocele is covered by peritoneum and amnion and is associated with chromosomal and other congenital anomalies.

q.s: Gastroschisis results mainly from failure of which process?
e: Correct. Gastroschisis and omphalocele are lateral fold defects (omphalocele also reflects failed return of the midgut).

q.s: Bladder exstrophy results from failure of which embryologic fold to close?
e: Wrong. Not a ventral wall fold.
Correct. Caudal fold failure causes bladder exstrophy.

q.s: A 3-month-old infant with congenital hypothyroidism has a soft bulge at the umbilicus covered by skin that protrudes when crying and reduces easily. What is the most likely course?
o: It indicates a vitelline duct fistula
Spontaneous closure is likely for small defects
It contains liver and is an omphalocele
e: Wrong. Small defects usually close spontaneously.
Correct. A congenital umbilical hernia from delayed umbilical ring closure often closes on its own.

q.s: Which feature distinguishes omphalocele from gastroschisis?
o: Omphalocele is covered by peritoneum and amnion
Omphalocele is to the right of the cord
Gastroschisis protrudes through the umbilical ring
e: Wrong. Gastroschisis is to the right.

q.s: A newborn drools, chokes and turns blue with the first feeding. A nasogastric tube cannot be passed into the stomach, and chest radiography shows the tube coiled in the upper esophagus with a prominent gastric air bubble. The pregnancy was complicated by polyhydramnios. Diagnosis?
o: Esophageal atresia with distal tracheoesophageal fistula
e: Wrong. NG tube passes; presents later with recurrent pneumonia.
Correct. The most common type (85%); air enters the stomach through the distal fistula.
Wrong. NG tube passes; double bubble.

q.s: Why does esophageal atresia cause polyhydramnios?
o: The fetus cannot swallow amniotic fluid
e: Correct. Normally swallowed fluid is absorbed in the gut.

q.s: A neonate with a tracheoesophageal fistula also has vertebral anomalies and a radial ray defect. Which association should be evaluated?
e: Correct. Vertebral, Anal atresia, Cardiac, TE fistula, Renal, Limb anomalies.
Wrong. Coloboma, heart, choanal atresia, growth, genital, ear.

q.s: A 4-month-old has recurrent pneumonia and coughing with feeds. A nasogastric tube passes easily into the stomach. Which anomaly is most likely?
e: Correct. The esophagus is continuous, so diagnosis is delayed; feeds pass into the trachea.
Wrong. NG tube would not pass.
Wrong. NG tube would not pass.

q.s: A firstborn 4-week-old boy has projectile nonbilious vomiting after every feed and is hungry afterward. An olive-shaped mass is felt in the epigastrium. Which acid-base disturbance is expected?
e: Correct. Loss of gastric HCl and volume contraction cause this in hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.

q.s: An infant treated with erythromycin at 1 week of age develops projectile vomiting at 3 weeks. What is the treatment of the likely condition?
e: Correct. Macrolide exposure is associated with hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, treated by surgical incision of the pyloric muscle.

q.s: How is hypertrophic pyloric stenosis confirmed?
o: Ultrasound showing a thickened, elongated pylorus

q.s: A newborn with Down syndrome has bilious vomiting on the first day of life. Abdominal radiography shows a "double bubble" with no distal gas. What is the embryologic cause?
o: Failure of the duodenal lumen to recanalize from the solid cord stage
Vascular accident in the SMA territory
e: Correct. Duodenal atresia is associated with Down syndrome.

q.s: A newborn has bilious vomiting and abdominal distension. Radiographs show a "triple bubble" and a gasless colon. The mother used cocaine during pregnancy. Mechanism?
o: Disruption of mesenteric blood flow causing ischemic necrosis and segmental resorption
Thick meconium from CFTR mutation alone
e: Correct. Jejunal and ileal atresia result from SMA disruption; vasoconstrictive drugs and smoking are risk factors.
Wrong. Meconium ileus, though CF is associated with atresia.

q.s: Jejunal and ileal atresia is associated with which conditions?
Which feature distinguishes duodenal atresia from hypertrophic pyloric stenosis?
o: Duodenal atresia has a palpable olive
Duodenal atresia presents in the first 1–2 days with bilious vomiting; pyloric stenosis presents at 2–6 weeks with nonbilious vomiting
Pyloric stenosis is associated with Down syndrome
e: Wrong. Usually bilious (obstruction distal to the ampulla).

q.s: In esophageal atresia with distal TEF, why does the infant become cyanotic during feeding?
o: Laryngospasm to protect against aspiration of refluxed contents
e: Correct. Cyanosis is secondary to laryngospasm.

q.s: A fetus has the heart located outside the chest wall through a sternal defect. Failure of which embryologic fold closure causes this?
e: Correct. Rostral fold failure causes sternal defects such as ectopia cordis.

q.s: In pure esophageal atresia without a fistula, what does the abdominal radiograph show?
e: Correct. No air can reach the stomach.
